claim: Increasing age is the strongest predictor of risk of COVID-19 severity and mortality.
source: Increasing age is the strongest predictor of risk of COVID-19 severity and mortality.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established knowledge about COVID-19 epidemiology.

claim: Immunometabolic switch from glycolysis to ketolysis protects against inflammatory damage and influenza infection in adults.
source: Immunometabolic switch from glycolysis to ketolysis protects against inflammatory damage and influenza infection in adults.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about metabolic switches and their protective effects.

claim: When inoculated intranasally, mCoV is pneumotropic and recapitulates several clinical hallmarks of COVID-19 infection.
source: When inoculated intranasally, mCoV is pneumotropic and recapitulates several clinical hallmarks of COVID-19 infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have increased mortality compared to young mice.
source: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have increased mortality and higher systemic inflammation in the heart, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus, including neutrophilia and loss of γδ T cells in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have higher systemic inflammation in the heart, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus.
source: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have increased mortality and higher systemic inflammation in the heart, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus, including neutrophilia and loss of γδ T cells in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine measurements and tissue analysis data.

claim: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have neutrophilia in lungs.
source: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have increased mortality and higher systemic inflammation in the heart, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus, including neutrophilia and loss of γδ T cells in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased neutrophils.

claim: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have loss of γδ T cells in lungs.
source: Aged mCoV-A59-infected mice have increased mortality and higher systemic inflammation in the heart, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus, including neutrophilia and loss of γδ T cells in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis of lung immune cells.

claim: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice expands tissue protective γδ T cells.
source: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice expands tissue protective γδ T cells, deactivates the NLRP3 inflammasome, and decreases pathogenic monocytes in lungs of infected aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and scRNA-seq data from KD-fed mice.

claim: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice deactivates the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice expands tissue protective γδ T cells, deactivates the NLRP3 inflammasome, and decreases pathogenic monocytes in lungs of infected aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and gene expression data showing reduced inflammasome activation.

claim: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice decreases pathogenic monocytes in lungs of infected aged mice.
source: Activation of ketogenesis in aged mice expands tissue protective γδ T cells, deactivates the NLRP3 inflammasome, and decreases pathogenic monocytes in lungs of infected aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis showing changes in monocyte populations.

claim: 80% of deaths due to COVID-19 in USA are in adults >65 years old.
source: Consequently, 80% of deaths due to COVID-19 in USA are in adults >65 years old (https://www.cdc.gov/), and aging is the strongest factor to increase infection fatality (Pastor-Barriuso et al., 2020; Perez-Saez et al., 2021; Ward et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by CDC data and cited epidemiological studies.

claim: Aging is the strongest factor to increase infection fatality.
source: Consequently, 80% of deaths due to COVID-19 in USA are in adults >65 years old (https://www.cdc.gov/), and aging is the strongest factor to increase infection fatality (Pastor-Barriuso et al., 2020; Perez-Saez et al., 2021; Ward et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited epidemiological studies.

claim: Inability of mouse ACE2 to bind SARS-CoV-2 is a significant hurdle in understanding the basic mechanism of COVID-19.
source: Inability of mouse ACE2 to bind SARS-CoV-2 is a significant hurdle in understanding the basic mechanism of COVID-19.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about species-specific receptor binding.

claim: K18-hACE2 model of SARS-CoV-2 infection demonstrated that post-intranasal inoculation, animals develop lung inflammation and pneumonia driven by infiltration of monocytes, neutrophils, and T cells.
source: For example, epithelial cell-specific induction of hACE2 (K18-hACE2) as a model of SARS-CoV-2 infection demonstrated that post-intranasal inoculation, animals develop lung inflammation and pneumonia driven by infiltration of monocytes, neutrophils, and T cells (Winkler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Winkler et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection in HFH4/FOXJ1 promoter-driven hACE2 transgenic mice induces weight loss, lung inflammation, and approximately 50% mortality rate.
source: Also, initial studies that employ lung-ciliated epithelial cell-specific HFH4/FOXJ1 promoter-driven hACE2 transgenic mice show that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces weight loss, lung inflammation, and approximately 50% mortality rate, suggesting the usefulness of this model to understand the mechanism of immune dysregulation (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2020.

claim: AAV9-mediated expression of hACE2 in C57BL/6 mice causes a productive SARS-CoV-2 infection with >200-fold increase in viral RNA.
source: The delivery of hACE2 into the respiratory tract of C57BL/6 mice with AAV9 causes a productive infection as revealed by >200-fold increase in SARS-CoV-2 RNA and shows similar interferon gene expression signatures as COVID-19 patients (Israelow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Israelow et al., 2020.

claim: In young wild-type mice, AAV9-hACE2 model induces mild ARDS and does not cause neutrophilia, weight loss, or lethality.
source: However, in young wild-type mice, this model induces mild acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and does not cause neutrophilia, weight loss, or lethality (Israelow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Israelow et al., 2020.

claim: The mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) and SARS-CoV-2 are both ARDS-related beta coronaviruses with a high degree of homology.
source: The mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) and SARS-CoV-2 are both ARDS-related beta coronaviruses with a high degree of homology (Gorbalenya et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gorbalenya et al., 2020.

claim: mCoV-A59 utilizes the entry receptor CEACAM1, which is expressed on respiratory epithelium, enterocytes, endothelial cells, and neurons.
source: Importantly, mCoV-A59 utilizes the entry receptor CEACAM1, which is expressed not only on respiratory epithelium, but also on enterocytes, endothelial cells, and neurons, much like ACE2 (Godfraind et al., 1995), thus allowing the study of wide-ranging systemic impacts of infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Godfraind et al., 1995.

claim: MHV infection is known to cause hepatitis and encephalomyelitis.
source: The MHV infection is known to cause hepatitis and encephalomyelitis (Lavi et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lavi et al., 1984.

claim: Intranasal infection with mCoV-A59 is pneumotropic and causes ARDS in C57BL/6J animals.
source: Importantly, however, the intranasal infection with mCoV-A59 is pneumotropic and causes ARDS in C57BL/6J animals, while all other MHV strains require the A/J or type-I interferon-deficient background, for the development of severe disease (De Albuquerque et al., 2006; Khanolkar et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2014) limiting their use.
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Albuquerque et al., 2006; Khanolkar et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Aging-induced chronic inflammation in the absence of overt infections is predominantly driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: Aging-induced chronic inflammation in the absence of overt infections is predominantly driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome (Bauernfeind et al., 2016; Camell et al., 2017; Youm et al., 2013), a myeloid cell-expressed multiprotein complex that senses pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) to cause the processing and secretion of IL-1β and IL-18.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bauernfeind et al., 2016; Camell et al., 2017; Youm et al., 2013.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with increased levels of IL-18 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels.
source: There is increasing evidence that SARS-CoV-2 infection activates the NLRP3 inflammasome with increased levels of IL-18 and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels due to inflammasome-mediated pyroptotic cell death (Lucas et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lucas et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Increased glycolysis is associated with worsened COVID-19 outcome.
source: It is now known that increased glycolysis, which activates inflammasome, is associated with worsened COVID-19 outcome (Codo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Codo et al., 2020.

claim: The LD-0 infectious dose of mCoV-A59 in adult mice (PFU 7e3) caused 100% lethality in aged mice.
source: The LD-0 infectious dose of mCoV-A59 in adult (PFU 7e3) caused 100% lethality in aged mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Aged mice displayed greater weight loss after mCoV-A59 infection compared to adults.
source: Aged mice displayed greater weight loss (Figure 1C), hypoxemia (Figure 1D), and anorexia (Figure 1E), without a significant difference in viral load in lungs (Figure 1F) after infection (PFU 7e2) when compared to adults.
evidence: This is supported by weight change data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Aged mice displayed hypoxemia after mCoV-A59 infection compared to adults.
source: Aged mice displayed greater weight loss (Figure 1C), hypoxemia (Figure 1D), and anorexia (Figure 1E), without a significant difference in viral load in lungs (Figure 1F) after infection (PFU 7e2) when compared to adults.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen saturation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Aged mice displayed anorexia after mCoV-A59 infection compared to adults.
source: Aged mice displayed greater weight loss (Figure 1C), hypoxemia (Figure 1D), and anorexia (Figure 1E), without a significant difference in viral load in lungs (Figure 1F) after infection (PFU 7e2) when compared to adults.
evidence: This is supported by food intake data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no significant difference in viral load in lungs between aged and adult mice after mCoV-A59 infection.
source: Aged mice displayed greater weight loss (Figure 1C), hypoxemia (Figure 1D), and anorexia (Figure 1E), without a significant difference in viral load in lungs (Figure 1F) after infection (PFU 7e2) when compared to adults.
evidence: This is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Aged mice had significant reductions in the percentage of CD4 cells in the lung compared to adult controls at steady state and after infection.
source: Immune profiling of the lung revealed that aged mice had significant reductions both in the percentage of CD4 cells and in the CD4:CD8 ratio in the lung compared to adult controls at steady state and after infection (Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Aged mice had significant reductions in the CD4:CD8 ratio in the lung compared to adult controls at steady state and after infection.
source: Immune profiling of the lung revealed that aged mice had significant reductions both in the percentage of CD4 cells and in the CD4:CD8 ratio in the lung compared to adult controls at steady state and after infection (Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: γδ T cell numbers in the lung were significantly increased at steady state in aged mice compared to adult mice.
source: Interestingly, while ϒδ T cell numbers in the lung were significantly increased at steady state in aged mice compared to adult mice, both the proportion and number of ϒδ T cells in the lung were dramatically reduced only in aged mice after infection compared to adult mice (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Both the proportion and number of γδ T cells in the lung were dramatically reduced only in aged mice after infection compared to adult mice.
source: Interestingly, while ϒδ T cell numbers in the lung were significantly increased at steady state in aged mice compared to adult mice, both the proportion and number of ϒδ T cells in the lung were dramatically reduced only in aged mice after infection compared to adult mice (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Aged mice had significantly increased neutrophils in the lung post-infection with a trend toward increase in neutrophils at steady state.
source: Analyses of the myeloid compartment revealed that aged mice had significantly increased neutrophils in the lung post-infection with a trend toward increase in neutrophils at steady state (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Aging increased Ly6Chi monocytes, which rose further post-infection.
source: Aging increased Ly6Chi monocytes, which rose further post-infection (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The frequency and number of CD64+MerTK+ cells were highest in infected aged mice.
source: Moreover, the frequency and number of CD64+MerTK+ cells were highest in infected aged mice (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), while no significant differences were observed in the total population of alveolar or interstitial macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F) in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the total population of alveolar or interstitial macrophages in lungs between aged and adult mice.
source: Moreover, the frequency and number of CD64+MerTK+ cells were highest in infected aged mice (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), while no significant differences were observed in the total population of alveolar or interstitial macrophages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F) in lungs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the dissemination of viral particles in pneumocytes in lungs.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the dissemination of the viral particles in pneumocytes in lungs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Following mCoV-A59 inoculation, pathology analyses revealed perivascular inflammation, perivascular edema, and increased perivascular collagen/fibrosis that is more severe in the 20–24 month mCoV-A59 infected mice.
source: Interestingly, following mCoV-A59 inoculation, pathology analyses by hematoxylin and eosin (H and E) and MSB staining, in both 6 month and 20–24 month old mice, revealed perivascular inflammation (arrows, arrowhead) as well as perivascular edema (*) and increased perivascular collagen/fibrosis (MSB, blue) that is more severe in the 20–24 month mCoV-A59 infected mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lungs of aged mice infected with mCoV-A59 had increased foci of inflammation, immune cell infiltration, perivascular edema, hyaline membrane formation and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, organizing pneumonia, interstitial pneumonitis, and occasional hemorrhage and microthrombi, affecting approximately 75% of the lungs.
source: Taken together, consistent with ARDS, the lungs of aged mice infected with mCoV-A59 had increased foci of inflammation, immune cell infiltration, perivascular edema, hyaline membrane formation and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, organizing pneumonia, interstitial pneumonitis, and occasional hemorrhage and microthrombi, affecting approximately 75% of the lungs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Old mice infected with mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating IL-1β compared to young animals.
source: Compared to young animals, old mice infected with equivalent doses of mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating IL-1β, TNFα, IL-6, and MCP-1 (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), without affecting MIP-1β (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by serum cytokine measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Old mice infected with mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating TNFα compared to young animals.
source: Compared to young animals, old mice infected with equivalent doses of mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating IL-1β, TNFα, IL-6, and MCP-1 (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), without affecting MIP-1β (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by serum cytokine measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Old mice infected with mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating IL-6 compared to young animals.
source: Compared to young animals, old mice infected with equivalent doses of mCoV-A59 displayed significant increase in circulating IL-1β, TNFα, IL-6, and MCP-1 (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D), without affecting MIP-1β (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by serum cytokine measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Infection with mCoV-A59 caused increased cardiac inflammation in old mice as evaluated by greater number of infiltrating CD68+ myeloid cells.
source: Similar to COVID-19, infection with mCoV-A59 caused increased cardiac inflammation in old mice as evaluated by greater number of infiltrating CD68+ myeloid cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: mCoV-A59 RNA was detectable in visceral adipose tissue (VAT).
source: Interestingly, consistent with the prior findings that adipose tissue can harbor several viruses (Damouche et al., 2015), the mCoV-A59 RNA was detectable in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Damouche et al., 2015.

claim: VAT of aged infected mice had significantly higher mRNA levels of IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 compared to young mice.
source: Despite similar viral loads, VAT of aged infected mice had significantly higher mRNA levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 (Figure 3F–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Aging is associated with increases in inflammasome activation.
source: Moreover, consistent with prior work, aging is associated with increases in inflammasome activation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I and references to prior work.

claim: Infection with mCoV-A59 enhanced caspase-1 cleavage in old mice.
source: Infection with mCoV-A59 further enhanced caspase-1 cleavage (p20 active heterodimer) as well as expression of inflammasome components, Casp1 and Nlrp3, in old mice (Figure 3I–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: mCoV-A59 was detectable in the hypothalamus.
source: In addition, similar to SARS-CoV-2 invasiveness in central nervous system (CNS), the mCoV-A59 was detectable in the hypothalamus (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The hypothalamus of aged infected mice showed increased mRNA expression of TNFα and caspase-1 compared to adults.
source: Compared to adults, the hypothalamus of aged infected mice showed increased mRNA expression of TNFα and caspase-1 (Figure 3M,N, Figure 3—figure supplement 1M,N) with no significant differences in IL-1β, IL-6 (Figure 3O,P, Figure 3—figure supplement 1O,P), and NLRP3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3M,N.

claim: mCoV-A59 infection completely abolished the expression of pre-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the hypothalamus.
source: However, mCoV-A59 infection completely abolished the expression of pre-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the hypothalamus, a transcript expressed by POMC neurons, which is involved in the control of the autonomic nervous system and integrative physiology.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data from the hypothalamus.

claim: BHB treatment reduced pro and active cleaved IL-1β (p17) in mCoV-A59 infected BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, BHB treatment reduced pro and active cleaved IL-1β (p17) in both conditions when protein level was measured in the supernatant (Figure 4A,B) and cell lysate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Post-mCoV-A59 infection, BHB reduced the oligomerization of ASC.
source: Mechanistically, post-mCoV-A59 infection, the BHB reduced the oligomerization of ASC, which is an adaptor protein required for the assembly of the inflammasome complex (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing ASC oligomerization in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Compared to chow-fed animals, old KD-fed mice achieved mild physiological ketosis between 0.6 and 1 mM over the course of infection for 1 week.
source: Despite mCoV-A59's known effects in causing hepatic inflammation (Navas et al., 2001), we observed that compared to chow-fed animals, old KD-fed mice achieved mild physiological ketosis between 0.6 and 1 mM over the course of infection for 1 week (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by BHB measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and citation to Navas et al., 2001.

claim: Young mice fed KD prior to infection showed improved survival compared to chow-fed controls.
source: Interestingly, compared to chow-fed controls, young mice fed KD prior to infection showed improved survival (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Old mice fed KD were not protected from death caused by high-dose mCoV-A59-induced infection.
source: However, old mice fed KD were not protected from death caused by high-dose mCoV-A59-induced infection (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: KD-fed mice inoculated with mCoV-A59 had significantly reduced mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus.
source: Consistent with the improved clinical outcome and protection afforded by ketone bodies in infected mice, we found that KD-fed mice inoculated with mCoV-A59 had significantly reduced mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-6 in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: KD significantly lowered NLRP3 and caspase-1 mRNA in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus in aged mice infected with mCoV-A59.
source: Interestingly, in the aging mouse model of mCoV-A59 infection, KD significantly lowered NLRP3 and caspase-1 mRNA in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus (Figure 5D,E), inflammasome activation in VAT (Figure 5F,G), and decreased myeloid cell infiltration in heart (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: KD decreased inflammasome activation in VAT in aged mice infected with mCoV-A59.
source: Interestingly, in the aging mouse model of mCoV-A59 infection, KD significantly lowered NLRP3 and caspase-1 mRNA in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus (Figure 5D,E), inflammasome activation in VAT (Figure 5F,G), and decreased myeloid cell infiltration in heart (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: KD decreased myeloid cell infiltration in heart in aged mice infected with mCoV-A59.
source: Interestingly, in the aging mouse model of mCoV-A59 infection, KD significantly lowered NLRP3 and caspase-1 mRNA in lung, VAT, and hypothalamus (Figure 5D,E), inflammasome activation in VAT (Figure 5F,G), and decreased myeloid cell infiltration in heart (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: KD feeding rescued mCoV-A59-induced depletion of γδ T cell in lungs of aged mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that KD feeding rescued mCoV-A59-induced depletion of ϒδ T cell in lungs of aged mice (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: scRNA-sequencing found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused significant increase in goblet cells.
source: The scRNA-sequencing of whole-lung tissues (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused significant increase in goblet cells (Figure 6B), expansion of ϒδ T cells (Figure 6B) and significant decrease in proliferative cell subsets and monocyte populations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: scRNA-sequencing found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused expansion of γδ T cells.
source: The scRNA-sequencing of whole-lung tissues (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused significant increase in goblet cells (Figure 6B), expansion of ϒδ T cells (Figure 6B) and significant decrease in proliferative cell subsets and monocyte populations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: scRNA-sequencing found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused significant decrease in proliferative cell subsets and monocyte populations.
source: The scRNA-sequencing of whole-lung tissues (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) found that KD feeding in old infected mice caused significant increase in goblet cells (Figure 6B), expansion of ϒδ T cells (Figure 6B) and significant decrease in proliferative cell subsets and monocyte populations (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: KD in aging significantly increased genes associated with reduced inflammation in γδ T cells.
source: We found that KD in aging significantly increased the genes associated with reduced inflammation (Figure 6D), increased lipoprotein remodeling and downregulation of TLR signaling, Plk1 and aurora B signaling pathways in ϒδ T cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: KD in aging increased lipoprotein remodeling and downregulation of TLR signaling, Plk1 and aurora B signaling pathways in γδ T cells.
source: We found that KD in aging significantly increased the genes associated with reduced inflammation (Figure 6D), increased lipoprotein remodeling and downregulation of TLR signaling, Plk1 and aurora B signaling pathways in ϒδ T cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: RNA-sequencing revealed that lung γδ T cells from ketogenic mCoV-A59-infected old mice displayed elevated respiratory electron transport and complex I biogenesis.
source: Furthermore, RNA-sequencing revealed that lung ϒδ T cells from ketogenic mCoV-A59-infected old mice displayed elevated respiratory electron transport and complex I biogenesis (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ketogenesis-induced change in the monocyte compartment was driven by a loss of cluster 1 characterized by high levels of Chil3, Lmna, Il1r2, Lcn2, Cd33, Cd24a.
source: Strikingly, ketogenesis-induced change in the monocyte compartment was driven by a loss of cluster 1 (characterized by high levels of Chil3, Lmna, Il1r2, Lcn2, Cd33, Cd24a, Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G,H).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: γδ T cells were severely depleted in COVID-19 patients in two highly variable cohorts.
source: Our findings assume strong clinical significance as recent studies demonstrate that γδ T cells were severely depleted in COVID-19 patients in two highly variable cohorts, and disease progression was correlated with near ablation of Vγ9Vδ2 cells that are dominant subtype of circulating γδ T cells (Laing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laing et al., 2020.

claim: Disease progression in COVID-19 was correlated with near ablation of Vγ9Vδ2 cells that are dominant subtype of circulating γδ T cells.
source: Our findings assume strong clinical significance as recent studies demonstrate that γδ T cells were severely depleted in COVID-19 patients in two highly variable cohorts, and disease progression was correlated with near ablation of Vγ9Vδ2 cells that are dominant subtype of circulating γδ T cells (Laing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laing et al., 2020.

claim: SARS-CoV open-reading frame 3a (ORF3a) and ORF8b activates the NLRP3 inflammasome.
source: The SARS-CoV open-reading frame 3a (ORF3a) and ORF8b activates the NLRP3 inflammasome (Siu et al., 2019) by inducing ER stress and lysosomal damage (Shi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Siu et al., 2019 and Shi et al., 2019.

claim: Ability of bats to harbor multiple viruses including coronaviruses is due to splice variants in the LRR domain of NLRP3, which prevents inflammasome-mediated inflammatory damage.
source: Moreover, ability of bats to harbor multiple viruses including coronaviruses is due to splice variants in the LRR domain of NLRP3, which prevents inflammasome-mediated inflammatory damage (Ahn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahn et al., 2019.

claim: MHV-A59 activates the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro BMDM.
source: Recent study shows that MHV-A59 also activates the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro BMDM (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2020.

claim: Severe cases of COVID-19 are accompanied with dysregulation of monocyte populations with increased level of S100A8/A9 or calprotectin.
source: In addition, severe cases of COVID-19 are accompanied with dysregulation of monocyte populations with increased level of S100A8/A9 or calprotectin (Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Silvin et al., 2020), which can prime and induce the inflammasome activation (Goldberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schulte-Schrepping et al., 2020; Silvin et al., 2020; Goldberg et al., 2017.

claim: Ketone bodies are produced during starvation to support the survival of host by serving as an alternative energy substrate when glycogen reserves are depleted.
source: Ketone bodies, BHB, and acetoacetate are produced during starvation to support the survival of host by serving as an alternative energy substrate when glycogen reserves are depleted (Newman and Verdin, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Newman and Verdin, 2017.

claim: Macrophage oxidation of liver-derived AcAc was essential for protection against liver fibrosis.
source: For example, stable isotope tracing revealed that macrophage oxidation of liver-derived AcAc was essential for protection against liver fibrosis (Puchalska et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Puchalska et al., 2019.

claim: KD-mediated enhancement of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation is required for protection against flu infection.
source: These results are consistent with a previous study reporting that KD-mediated enhancement of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation is required for protection against flu infection. In the study, increasing BHB by feeding ketone esters could not mimic the effect of KD (Goldberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2019.
